questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The language spoken both at the university and in the public sphere, the financial aspect/living costs of the area, while also seeking an urban area.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The education itself was very lacklustre and disappointing. The university has a completely different standard and way of life, which of course is to be expected, however I felt like I was back in high school. Having said that, the experience itself was amazing and I learned a lot from it. Particularly on the language front, given that I can now confidently say I speak Spanish fluently both colloquial but also academic.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The University of Valencia is highly equipped to deal with exchange students and have an administration I envy, given that my home university does not provide the same service. While there's still a learning curve to their systems, particularly their email system stemming from 1998, everybody working there do their best to accommodate you and provide information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Meetings, mails, and such for international students at the university. Of course the assistance only pertains to university matters and other matters are up to you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was okay. However, many accommodations are very 'at the moment' meaning that they when I first searched for a place back in October, there was nothing available which didn't require me to move in immediately.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: beware there are a lot of scam firms such as SoyErasmus which will place you in a run-down apartment and won't pay back the deposit.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you come from Denmark/Copenhagen. Expect the housing to not be as new/nice as you may be used to. However, most places have bidets and baths which is pretty nice.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's a bit of legwork figuring out what classes work which what classes, but after that you are simply given a time to show up at the administration and they you talk about what classes you wish to have.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always write to the administration or show up at the secretary who'll provide information.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very, I had to change 2 or 3 classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be flexible.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Exams are written in hand, not on computer.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: 5 Courses, each 6 ETCS points.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It certainly felt like I was back in high school. For me, I was very sad about the teaching style simply because they were obviously competent and smart educators, however, their teaching style was simply to provide us with information. You had to simply memorise everything and you didn't use the information in a critical manner, nor were you given reason for why it was important to know or remember what you were told. For example, I took a class in art history, where our teacher had a module on islamic art in Spain and how some churches are old mosques and how you can tell - we could have talked about the political part of it, the reconquistas and so on or even the interesting differences between islamic art not portraying persons versus christian art which does. But not, we were simply told that islamic art doesn't portray persons without our educator going into detail about why this is, given that there are obvious religious/cultural reasons for it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Historia del arte, lecturas contemporáneas hispanoamericanas, Español de América, Español coloquial, El español y las lenguas del mundo hispánico

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Español de América is very interesting and la profesora Milagros Aleza Izquierdo is a really lovely woman. The subject itself isn't very difficult, especially if you have had phonetics prior to the class, but it's very interesting to hear and learn about both the phonetic, but also the lexical differences in language between different Spanish speaking nations. 

I would also recommend Español coloquial, I took this class in the international class so the educators are aware of our limits as students. Here our educators were Marta Pilar Montañez Mesas and Antonio Briz Gomez. Marta is a delight and a really engaging educator. Antonio is the expert of the subject in all of Spain and it's great to have him as educator. Here the focus is on sociolinguistics, colloquial language, and transcriptions.

I personally prefer studying history and literature, normally as those subjects interest me - but I would not recommend to do that here, as they do not engage the students in a meaningful way, making it simply boring.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Got my phone stolen twice. Luckily I had my insurance. 

Ended up spending a lot more on partying, cabs, and such than expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Difficult to expand on given that the Russia/Ukraine crisis began during my stay, so we did experience quite a surge in food prices and such. However, cabs are very inexpensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Cannot comment as I did not attend any.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Lots of different sports team.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Bachata con Kevin y Lucía, it's dancing in the park and a lot of fun. I would go there every time and usually we'd go to a bar afterwards to party. If you like dancing there's also Supersalseros, with salsa, bachata, kizumba and a bunch of different events.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The food, the parties. Not the Erasmus parties, the music is shit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't. I socialised with the locals through the dancing events I went to, because there were just so many non-local students at my university the locals didn't want to mingle with us that much.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You don't have to say "thank you" as much haha.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: All of it. People are nice, the food is amazing, the music is good.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't do it for the academic experience, do it for everything else. Do your best to mingle with locals, enjoy the beach and the food.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: They take attendance in a lot of classes.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Simply getting to speak Spanish so much and getting to know and enjoy life with such wonderful people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding the energy to care about class, when it was boring.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
